topics.explain: Para looks ahead to a goal: purpose (para ahorrar = in order to save), recipient (para ti), deadline (para el lunes), destination (sale para Lima). Por looks back at a cause or a route: reason (por orgullo = out of pride), through/along (por la rambla), exchange or price (por diez euros), part of the day (por la mañana), 'per'. Watch out: English 'for' can be either: 'thanks for' = gracias por, 'for you' = para ti.
examples: Tomás se fue a Estados Unidos para ahorrar.
Tomás went to the United States to save money.
Por orgullo dejé de preguntar por él.
Out of pride I stopped asking about him.
Caminaron por la rambla junto al río.
They walked along the promenade by the river.

questions.q: Complete: Gracias ___ ayudarme. Este pastel es ___ ti.
questions.why: Gracias por: por gives the reason you are thankful. Es para ti: para marks the recipient.

questions.q: Complete: Marta ahorró durante un año ___ viajar a Montevideo.
questions.why: Purpose ('in order to') is para + infinitive. Por viajar would mean 'because of travelling', which changes the sense.

topics.explain: Use the preterite for actions in a finished time: ayer, el lunes pasado, en 2019 (Ayer hablé con ella). Use the present perfect for a period that includes now (hoy, esta semana, este año, nunca, ya, todavía no) or a past action whose result matters now (Este año he leído mucho). Watch out: never use the present perfect with a finished time (*ayer he hablado). In much of Latin America the preterite is also normal for today (Hoy hablé con ella).
examples: Ayer recibí una carta de Marta.
Yesterday I got a letter from Marta.
Este año he leído muchos libros.
I've read a lot of books this year.
¿Has estado alguna vez en Granada? —Sí, estuve allí en 2019.
Have you ever been to Granada? —Yes, I was there in 2019.

questions.q: Complete: Joaquín ___ veinticuatro años el jueves pasado.
questions.why: El jueves pasado is a finished time, so the preterite is required (cumplió). The present perfect can't go with a finished past time, and the participle never ends in -a after haber.

questions.q: Which time expression can NOT be used with the present perfect (he visto)?
questions.why: El lunes pasado is a finished period, which needs the preterite (vi). Hoy, este año and nunca include the present, so the present perfect works with them.

topics.topic: Subjunctive after para que, antes de que, sin que
topics.explain: Some linking words always take the subjunctive because the action is not (yet) a fact: para que (so that), antes de que (before), sin que (without), a menos que (unless). In a past context use the imperfect subjunctive: Salió antes de que empezara a llover. Watch out: if both parts share the same subject, use the infinitive: Ahorro para viajar (not *para que viaje); Salí sin hacer ruido.
examples: Te lo digo para que no te preocupes.
I'm telling you so that you don't worry.
Salió antes de que empezara a llover.
He left before it started raining.
Se fue sin que nadie lo viera.
He left without anyone seeing him.

questions.q: Complete: Te dejo la llave para que ___ cuando quieras.
questions.why: Para que always takes the subjunctive: entres. The infinitive (para entrar) is only possible when the subject is the same in both parts.

options: Quiero hablar contigo antes de que te vas.
Quiero hablar contigo antes de que te irás.
Quiero hablar contigo antes de te vayas.
Quiero hablar contigo antes de que te vayas.
questions.why: Antes de que always takes the subjunctive (te vayas), and both de and que are needed before a conjugated verb.

topics.topic: Object pronoun order: se lo, me la
topics.explain: With two object pronouns, the indirect one (to whom) comes first: me lo, te la, nos los. Le or les becomes se before lo, la, los, las: le doy la cartera → se la doy (never *le la). Both go before a conjugated verb (se la devuelvo) or are attached to an infinitive, gerund or affirmative command (quiero devolvérsela, dámelo). Watch out: when you attach them, add a written accent to keep the original stress.
examples: Quería devolvérsela hoy mismo.
I wanted to give it back to you today.
¿La cartera? Se la di a Tomás.
The wallet? I gave it to Tomás.
No me lo digas todavía.
Don't tell me yet.

questions.q: Replace the nouns with pronouns: Inés le devolvió la cartera a Tomás.
questions.why: Indirect before direct, and le becomes se before la: se la. The direct pronoun must agree with la cartera (feminine), so not lo.

questions.q: How do you say 'Give it to me' (tú; it = el libro)?
questions.why: Affirmative command + indirect (me) + direct (lo), attached, with an accent: dámelo. Me lo da is a statement ('he gives it to me'), and the direct object for el libro is lo.

topics.explain: Se + a third-person verb says what is done without saying who does it: Aquí se habla español (Spanish is spoken here). With a noun, the verb agrees with it: se vende una casa / se venden casas. With no noun, it means people in general: En este barrio se vive bien. Watch out: English passives and 'you/people/they' sentences often become se in Spanish, not ser + participle: ¿Cómo se dice...? = How do you say...?
examples: Es una bebida que se comparte.
It's a drink that is shared.
Se venden cuadernos hechos a mano.
Handmade notebooks for sale.
¿Cómo se dice «awkward» en español?
How do you say 'awkward' in Spanish?

questions.q: Complete the sign: Se ___ pisos en el centro.
questions.why: With passive se, the verb agrees with the noun: pisos is plural, so se venden. Se vende pisos is a common mistake.

questions.q: What does 'En este barrio se vive bien' mean?
options: People live well in this neighborhood.
He lives well in this neighborhood.
This neighborhood lives well by itself.
They lived well in this neighborhood.
questions.why: Impersonal se with no noun refers to people in general: 'people / you live well here'. It is present tense and doesn't refer to one specific person.

topics.topic: Verb phrases: llevar + gerund, acabar de, volver a, dejar de
topics.explain: Spanish uses verb + infinitive/gerund combinations for time and aspect. Llevar + time + gerund = 'have been doing for': Llevo dos años trabajando aquí. Acabar de + infinitive = 'have just': Acabo de llegar. Volver a + infinitive = 'do again'. Dejar de + infinitive = 'stop doing'. Seguir + gerund = 'keep doing'. Watch out: 'I've been working here for two years' is Llevo dos años trabajando aquí or Trabajo aquí desde hace dos años, not a word-for-word translation.
examples: Marcos llevaba tres años trabajando como enfermero.
Marcos had been working as a nurse for three years.
No vamos a volver a ser extraños.
We aren't going to be strangers again.
Dejé de preguntar por él.
I stopped asking about him.

questions.q: Complete: Marcos ___ tres años trabajando en el hospital.
questions.why: Llevar + time + gerund expresses how long an action has (or had) been going on. The other verbs don't form this structure (with hacer you'd say hacía tres años que trabajaba).

questions.q: What does 'Acabo de recibir tu carta' mean?
options: I'm about to receive your letter.
questions.why: Acabar de + infinitive means 'to have just done'. 'About to' is estar a punto de; 'finally' is por fin.
